posts.title: Forum for posting comments on week 1-2 readings (due Sep 21)

items.name: 鍾祐霖
items.note:
Evaluation is the worst form of HCI research except all those other forms that have been tried

This essay is aiming to address two things. The first one is to rectify some misunderstanding of evaluation in the field of HCI, and the second one is to emphasis that even though most of the methods seems not good enough for evaluation, it’s still better than researchers or designers’ subjective opinion.

The most impressive aspect of the author for me is that he said the value of evaluation, or experimental study, isn't just about the conclusion of the test, but more broadly about the deeper understanding alongside the process of evaluation. The insight gained or inspired in the process may lead to improving the idea or coming up with some whole new ideas.

By this understanding of the purpose of evaluation methods in HCI realm, I know that the study of HCI isn’t just focusing on proving or disproving a theory or design, but also to be inspired and come up with more ideas alongside.

items.name: 王玉美
items.note:
Quantifying User Research 

This article has summarized the types of quantitative method of Human Computer Interaction Research. Moreover, this article has clearly explain which quantitative research is good for which HCI research topic and how we are going to get the data comprehensively. Now, I understand how quantitative research method has played a role in Human Computer Interaction research field. Furthermore, this paper has mentioned clearly of each objective (what you will likely to get) from all the method you are doing. For example, Rating Scale. It allows the researchers to get an insight about the comparison of responses to different product. By knowing all the reason a quantitative research method to be used, we are able to easily decide which method is suitable for our research topic. Therefore, we are able to get the meaningful and interesting data from those methods. 

In my own opinion, I think this paper is indeed a good paper to help people who are not coming HCI research field to get to know about how to quantify the HCI research. To me, normally people that are coming from CS department or any department are less likely to be interested in qualitative kind of research, like HCI more likely is doing, instead, they are more confident in using the number to understand phenomenon  and it is indeed very helpful for a relatively young research field, HCI, to attract more people to work on HCi research field and to develop this kind of research field.

items.name: 王玉美
items.note:
Purchase Book _ Preface – Ch 1.

This book explains what does HCI idea and how to come up with HCI topic. HCI idea simple means an idea that consists human and technology and definitely about their interaction. In HCI research field, there are 2 types of doing HCI tests: experiments and exploratory usability evaluations. The difference between these two approach is that experiments focuses on testing the new idea’s performances are better than the previous one. While, usability evaluation focuses on the explore if the idea is successful in practice.

It is hard to measure if the idea is good or not in HCI research. Even with the impressive rate of certain calculation, it is hard to say that these results are worth of the idea. Hence, this books has mentioned about how hard it is to come up with HCI research idea. However, this book chapter have roughly mentioned about the elements or points that should be considered. Lastly, I hope through this course, I will be able to come up with good HCI research and be wise n choosing the method for research and follow the guide provided in the resources given.

items.name: 蔡守恩
items.note:
Evaluation is the worst form of HCI research except all those other forms that have been tried


People may have some misunderstandings regarding the method, evaluation, in HCI researches and may argue that it’s insufficient, over-generalized or too less participants. But just like what the author, Shumin Zhai and Henry Lieberman, whose critique provoked the author to write this article, stated, doing user-interface researches is not like doing calculations. Since it’s the lack of strong theories or principles, we have to rely on evaluative method. 

I especially like the argument from the end of Henry Lieberman's essay. Exactly, we can't stop doing evaluation, but we can't merely rely on it, insist on it. What we are facing is the users, the humans, full of variances and having complicated and totally different mindset, we can't just control only one variances like the experiments people do in other fields. It's the most important and valuable that judgment from evaluation. I always keep thinking that what he stated: it's not just engineering questions, it's not the whole story. And may remind me that do not only focus the conclusions ,and besides, avoid "perfectly-user-interface". It's like you're trying to satisfy everyone's needs but it must obviously fail in the end because of significantly different cognitive styles and the most importantly,lack the artistry of design.

items.name: 楊馥名
items.note:
The readings share some interlocking insights that all tie in with each other. Zhai when emphasizing the need for evaluation insinuates that this necessity stems partly from the lack of strong existing models, theories, and laws in HCI. Support for this point is revealed in both the Purchase and MacKenzie readings: 

The history of HCI has implied that HCI has developed in such a way that it has expanded to become broader than is reasonably imaginable and encompasses a multitude of highly varying academic disciplines. This would contribute to the difficulty of establishing standardized and solid models, theories and laws in HCI because bridging together the individual beliefs and practices of such a large array of various disciplines is a very nuanced task.

Helen Purchase, apart from directly mentioning Zhai's article in agreement, emphasizes that even she can only explain the experimental evaluation practice using examples from her own discipline, which is one of the many involved in HCI. But she also mentions that the experimental principles themselves (core to the act of evaluation, as mentioned by Zhai) can be rigorously applied in other HCI areas which demonstrates evaluation is a core shared value that can bind the work of different HCI areas together effectively. This is also important because the variation in HCI-involved disciplines means that shared specific knowledge is distributed more sparsely across the entire realm of HCI and this concept even further discredits the sole use of judgment in design.

items.name: 盧俊言
items.note:
Quantifying User Research

This chapter introduces user research and how to generate quantifiable outcomes, especially emphasizing on usability testing. This is mainly because usability testing is a central activity, has been conducted and written extensively and has many same metrics as other research techniques, including completion rates, task times, errors, satisfaction data and user interface problems.

Data from user research won’t fall out of favor. The sample of users represents the population about which you make statement. In addition to minimize bias in sample as far as possible, representativeness is more important than randomness. Otherwise, when it comes to usability problems, dividing the number of occurrences or combining data is also important.

This article provides the basic knowledge of quantifying user research and some related properties, telling readers that something need to be noticed. When doing user research, people must take care of every parts of it and seek to minimize bias.

items.name: 李若彤
items.note:
Quantifying User Research

The reading extends my knowledge of user research, especially about usability testing. The most impressive aspect of the chapter that was the section of sample sizes. In my past view, sample sizes should be large (above 30) to use statistics. If sample sizes are below the standard, the researcher have to collect qualitative data to interpret the findings. However, in the section of Representativeness and Randomness writes: ‘Where possible seek to minimize systematic bias in your sample but remember that representativeness is more important than randomness.’ In other words, it is uncertain that sample sizes are the larger the better. The most important thing is representativeness.

Although the reading enhances my understanding, it is not enough. There are detailed descriptions and tips in other chapters. As for me, every students study in HCI should read the book, which serve as a base for future studies.

items.name: 張儷齡
items.note:
Quantifying User Research


Straight to say, this book will be one of my recommended books to someone who want to do user research, this is a good guide book of that. Once I did a small user experience project about tripnotice.com, a website which will analyse massive air tickets, restaurants, attractions, festive information and recommend valuable Itinerary for your self-guided tour, and what i am learned from that are entirely listed out in this article: What is usability testing, What metrics usually should be use and what is those metrics. They are the necessary basic ideas of the User Research. Among them I was impressed with 'Sample size and representativeness are actually different concepts'. I think data is the cornerstone of the user research, so it is important to remember that representative is more important than sample size. Another worth mentioning is the Task Time. It is just because it made me realize ‘Time until failure’ is a valuable metric, and our team Ignored before. That was really a pity.


Actually, I choose this article to be my first reading in this class because of the ‘Quantifying’ in the title. But I have started to regret that I did not read the book earlier now.

items.name: 林奕汝
items.note:
MacKenzie book. Chapter 1. Historical Context

This chapter talked about the history of HCI, including devices inventions, concept formulations, and the begin of empirical experiments/user studies. It helps me to clarify how different domain mixed into HCI and also answer the question I had: "What's the contribution can a CS person made in HCI?" There's a bunch of examples that CS/EE people use the power of technology to implement prototypes. The most encouraging example is how the first mouse invented. Most people can tell the eager of a natural way to control, but without the knowledge of engineering, they would never use voltage signals to achieve this goal.

items.name: 林奕汝
items.note: Zhai (2003) posted an article on his web-page. He proposed "Evaluation is the worst form of HCI research except all those other forms that have been tried". As we know nowadays, evaluation is necessary but never a final target. Evaluation is not a single standard process. There're many ways to do it depending on the case, situation, or the environment limitations. What I wonder is that whether the community maintained a note about all of the existing evaluation methods with their requirements and limitations. I believe that would be a efficient and helpful guideline for both students and new researchers.

items.name: 林奕汝
items.note:
Sauro & Lewis book. Chapter 2. Quantifying User Research 

In this chapter, the authors introduce the basic concept and process to conduct a quantitative user research. This article helped my understanding of usability especially. As they said there's no proper guideline for every products to follow. But some frequent tested terms are listed and I'd like to cut down the target products into the chatbots. Thus, the users have countable goals that I can put analysis on their reviews after using. After the analysis of reviews and getting lists of usability problems, a in-lab experiment can also be applied to get users' completion rates, errors, task times, task-level satisfaction, test-level satisfaction, and help access.

items.name: 林奕汝
items.note:
Purchase book. Chapter 1. Introduction “Assessing the worth of an HCI idea” 

The 1st chapter in this book go over the foundation of HCI and the value of it. People touch this field for their first time may feel that this introduction is too shallow and too broad. But HCI is actually such a broad area which can't introduce completely in only one chapter. Even the researchers in HCI can only master in some of the topics/domains listed in this chapter. Understanding the rich diversity in HCI and focusing on our own interests are the lessons I've learned.

items.name: 盧俊言
items.note:
Purchase Book_Preface – Ch1.

The preface gives an overview of HCI idea and different approaches to testing. It mainly discusses how to assess the worth of HCI idea. The first is by comparison and the second is by use. I think how to define whether an idea is good need to consider both evaluation. Judging from my current study, the new method we develop has two advantage. Each is better than different two kinds of traditional method. This is comparison. And researchers always have a pilot before formal experiment. Through this process participants can find out any problem of the experiment and give advises to researcher for modifying the idea. This is the other assessment by use. The final gives the key distinguishing features of these two types of HCI test. Experiments are comparative and focus on producing data to demonstrate the worth of an HCI idea. Evaluation are not comparative and focus on producing feedback to either improve a system or confirm its readiness for deployment.

items.name: 姚舜懷
items.note:
Quantifying User Research

This reading brings me clear insights into user research. They take many examples with emphasizing on usability testing. For example, A/B testing is a popular method for comparing different user interface and usability in industry. The method is easy to automatically collect the number of users who presented with each design so that it is straightforward to see which design is better. 
Again, the chapter is worth reading for who want to give a look about user quantitative research.

items.name: 劉  淨
items.note:
Puechase book: Ch1-Introduction :Assessing the worth of an HCI idea"

This reading presents an overview of HCI idea, HCI testing. In the author's perspective, and CHI idea is an idea that is implemented and used and involves interaction between humans and technology. An CHI idea needs to be tested by people. Their are two major ways to test an HCI idea: formal comparative experiments (or simply termed experiment) and exploratory usability evaluations (or termed usability studies). Formal comparative experiments are appropriate for ideas that have easily-found alternatives to be compared with and usually associated with well-defined tasks. In contrast, evaluations are appropriate for ideas that can support a wide range of use tasks and it is difficult to fine alternatives (ex., complex interactive system). Both of the methods can carry out summative result, which produces conclusion, and formative result, which makes recommendations for improvement. 

The overview gives a high level criteria for us to decide what kind of test to apply on an idea. And beside the two testing method, there are other research details that are crucial to presents the value of an idea, such as design  rationale, scenarios of use, existence proofs, and participatory critique.

items.name: 姚舜懷
items.note:
Introduction “Assessing the worth of an HCI idea” 

The chapter is recommended for who want to do HCI research but have few experience with HCI. It gives a high level assessment to think about if your HCI idea is worth to do. We can follow formal comparative experiments and exploratory usability evaluations mentioned in the chapter. Although the details of these experiments and evaluations are not mentioned, it still guides us how to dig deeper.

items.name: 劉  淨
items.note:
Quantifying User Research

This reading covers comprehensive concepts related to usability testing. There are two types of usability tests: formative tests and summative tests. Most of the usability tests are formative. There are two typical ways to do summative tests, which are benchmark and comparative. Them it discuss sample size, representativeness and randomness of samples, data collection method and data types. 
I feel like the testing methods presented in this article are common methods employed by HCI researcher in industry, but it also provides useful tips to conduct more rigorous studies within a research project.
